'''Alan Hall''' [[Fellow of the Royal Society|FRS]]<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal |last1=Machesky |first1=Laura M. |last2=Jaffe |first2=Aron B. |last3=Ridley FRS |first3=Anne J. |date=2024 |title=Alan Hall. 19 May 1952 — 3 May 2015 |journal=Biographical Memoirs of Fellows of the Royal Society |volume=77|pages=201–219 |doi=10.1098/rsbm.2023.0038 |doi-access=free }}</ref> (19 May 1952  – 3 May 2015) was a British [[cell biologist]] and a biology professor at the [[Sloan-Kettering Institute]], where he was chair of the Cell Biology program. Hall was elected a [[List of fellows of the Royal Society G, H, I|Fellow]] of the [[Royal Society]] in 1999.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.the-scientist.com/?articles.view/articleNo/42883/title/Prominent-Cell-Biologist-Dies/|title=Prominent Cell Biologist Dies}}</ref>

==Early life and education==
Hall was born in [[Barnsley]] in [[Yorkshire]]. He earned his BA in chemistry from [[Oxford University]]. He began his studies for a PhD at Oxford, but after two months he followed his major professor [[Jeremy R. Knowles]] to [[Harvard University]], where he earned a PhD in biochemistry in 1977.<ref>[http://www.ascb.org/ascb-post/in-memoriam-alan-hall-pioneer-in-rho-gtpases-and-chair-of-cell-biology-at-sloan-kettering/ In Memoriam: Alan Hall, Pioneer in Rho GTPases and Chair of Cell Biology at Sloan-Kettering]</ref> He then took [[postdoctoral]] fellowships in molecular biology at the [[University of Edinburgh]] and the [[University of Zurich]].<ref name="work">{{cite web|url=http://www.mskcc.org/research/lab/alan-hall/work|title=At Work: Cell Biology Program Chair Alan Hall|work=Memorial Sloan-Kettering Cancer Center|accessdate=2015-03-03|url-status=dead|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20150402095940/http://www.mskcc.org/research/lab/alan-hall/work|archivedate=2 April 2015|df=dmy-all}}</ref>

==Career and research==

Hall's PhD with Knowles was on the enzymology of [[β-lactamase]], which led to his first paper being published in [[Nature (journal)|Nature]] in 1976. He used strains of ''E. coli'' with mutated β-lactamase, an antibiotic resistance enzyme, and assayed their activity in the presence of benzylpenicillin and cephalosporin C. Direct selection on these mutants allowed catalytic properties of β-lactamase to be identified and allowed structure-function relationships of the enzyme to be researched further.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Hall|first1=Alan|last2=Knowles|first2=Jeremy|title=Directed selective pressure on a beta-lactamase to analyse molecular changes involved in development of enzyme function.|journal=Nature|date=23 December 1976|volume=264|issue=5588|pages=803–804|pmid=796732|doi=10.1038/264803a0|bibcode=1976Natur.264..803H|s2cid=4193701}}</ref> As a PhD student, Hall also published a paper on [[triosephosphate isomerase]] (TIM), which is a key enzyme in [[glycolysis]]. Specifically, he characterized the uncatalyzed interconversion of the two TIM substrates: [[dihydroxyacetone phosphate]] and [[glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate]].<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Hall|first1=Alan|last2=Knowles|first2=Jeremy|title=The uncatalyzed rates of enolization of dihydroxyacetone phosphate and of glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate in neutral aqueous solution. The quantitative assessment of the effectiveness of an enzyme catalyst.|journal=Biochemistry|date=1975|volume=14|issue=19|pages=4348-4352|pmid=1182103|doi=10.1021/bi00690a032}}</ref>  But as was later noted by [[John P. Richard]],<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Richard|first1=John|title=Acid–base catalysis of the elimination and isomerization reactions of triose phosphates.|journal=Journal of the American Chemical Society|date=1984|volume=106|issue=19|pages=4926-4936|doi=10.1021/ja00329a050}}</ref> Hall's analysis was compromised because he did not take into account the overriding β-elimination of inorganic phosphate from the enediol intermediate in the uncatalyzed reaction (unlike in the TIM-catalyzed reaction), forming [[methylglyoxal]].

In 1981, Hall went to work at [[Institute of Cancer Research|Institute for Cancer Research]] in London, where he stayed for 12 years. His work, in collaboration with his colleague and close friend [[Christopher Marshall (doctor)|Christopher Marshall]], made seminal contributions to our understanding of cell signalling in animal cells, in particular the role of [[Rho family of GTPases|Rho]] and [[Ras superfamily|Ras]] small [[GTPase]]s in regulating a variety of cellular functions such as proliferation, morphology and migration. In 1982, Hall helped identify transforming sequences in human sarcoma cell lines at the Institute for Cancer Research in London. DNA from a rhabdomyosarcoma cell line and a fibrosarcoma cell line transformed an NIH/3T3 mouse fibroblast cell line. After injection into mice, tumors started to form in as little as 10 days. Next, the transforming activities of the rhabdomyosarcoma and fibrosarcoma cell lines were measured after being digested with an array of [[endonuclease]]s. Further DNA testing showed that the transforming sequences in the two cancer cell lines were the same, and the gene was later characterised as [[Neuroblastoma RAS viral oncogene homolog|N-ras]], a member of the Ras gene family.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Marshall|first1=CJ|last2=Hall|first2=Allan|last3=Weiss|first3=RA|title=A transforming gene present in human sarcoma cell lines.|journal=Nature|year=1982|volume=299|pages=171–173|pmid=6287287|doi=10.1038/299171a0|issue=5879|bibcode=1982Natur.299..171M|s2cid=4342747}}</ref>

In 1986, Hall helped uncover properties of the human p21 protein, which is encoded by N-ras. GTPase activity of different mutant forms of p21, one cloned from a patient with myeloblastic leukaemia and one derived from in vitro mutagenesis, was measured. Results showed no correlation between the wild-type or mutant N-ras p21's GTPase activity and transforming potential. These findings were published in [[Molecular and Cellular Biology|Molecular and Cellular Biology (MCB)]].<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Trahey|first1=M|last2=Milley|first2=RJ|last3=Cole|first3=GE|last4=Innis|first4=M|last5=Patterson|first5=H|last6=Marshall|first6=CJ|last7=Hall|first7=A|last8=McCormick|first8=F|title=Biochemical and biological properties of the human N-ras p21 protein.|journal=Molecular and Cellular Biology|year=1987|volume=7|issue=1|pages=541–544|doi=10.1128/MCB.7.1.541|pmid=3550423|pmc=365100}}</ref>

Alan Hall showed the specificity of Rho in the stimulation of [[focal adhesion]]s and stress fibre formation in [[fibroblast]]s in the presence of extracellular factors in 1992. He first realised that the addition of bovine fetal calf serum (FCS) to Swiss 3T3 cells increased the polymerisation of actin and assembly of stress fibres. The immunofluorescence following the increase of [[vinculin]] and [[Talin (protein)|talin]], two cytoskeletal proteins, at the intracellular face of the plasma membrane with Val14rhoA microinjection showed the association of focal adhesions with the end of the new stress fibres. After size fractionation of FCS and analysis of the lipids that bound to serum albumin, the [[Lysophosphatidic acid|lysophosphatidic acid (LPA)]] was found to be responsible for the serum activity that induced stress fibre formation. The inhibition of Rho by C3 transferase ribosylation resulted in an inhibition of focal adhesion and stress fibre assembly, but had no effect on [[membrane ruffling]]. These findings were published in Cell and cited over 4000 times.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Ridley|first1=Anne|last2=Hall|first2=Alan|title=The small GTP-binding protein rho regulates the assembly of focal adhesions and actin stress fibers in response to growth factors|journal=Cell|date=7 August 1992|volume=70|issue=3|pages=389–399|doi=10.1016/0092-8674(92)90163-7|pmid=1643657|doi-access=}}</ref> In parallel with this experiment, Hall showed that the presence of [[Rac (GTPase)|Rac]], another Ras-related GTP-binding protein, is implicated in the regulation of the actin organisation in presence of extracellular growth factors. Immunofluorescence and antibody techniques were used to localise the mutant V12rac1 protein after being microinjected into the cytoplasm of confluent serum-starved Swiss 3T3 cells. The comparison with the normal cells showed that Rac1 stimulates actin filament production at the membrane, pinocytosis, and membrane ruffling. The inhibition of endogenous Rac function by mutants N17rac and V12rac1 prevented growth factor-induced membrane ruffling. In addition, the inactivation of Rho protein by [[ADP-ribosylation]] in Rac1 microinjection reduced the formation of actin stress fibres. Hall concluded that Rac and Rho are complementary for polymerised actin organisation. Indeed, Rho-dependent response is stimulated by the action of growth factors on Rac protein.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Ridley|first1=AJ|last2=Paterson|first2=HF|last3=Johnston|first3=CL|last4=Diekmann|first4=D|last5=Hall|first5=A|title=The small GTP-binding protein rac regulates growth factor-induced membrane ruffling.|journal=Cell|date=7 August 1992|volume=70|issue=3|pages=401–410|url=http://www.unboundmedicine.com/medline/citation/1643658/The_small_GTP_binding_protein_rac_regulates_growth_factor_induced_membrane_ruffling_|doi=10.1016/0092-8674(92)90164-8|pmid=1643658|doi-access=free|url-access=subscription}}</ref>

In 1993 he moved to [[University College London]], where he helped to create a MRC Cell Biology Unit, within the  Laboratory for Molecular Cell Biology ([https://www.ucl.ac.uk/life-sciences/lmcb LMCB]). In 2000, he became director of the MRC Laboratory for Molecular Cell Biology. 
 
In 2002, Alan Hall discerned the role of [[Gq alpha subunit|G<sub>aq</sub>]] in Rho signalling pathways. Prior to this publication, there were conflicting reports as to the role of G<sub>aq</sub> in cell signalling via Rho; some said that it was not able to induce Rho activation, and some said that it could. Using immunoblotting techniques, Hall showed that activation of endogenous G<sub>aq</sub> via [[G protein-coupled receptor|G protein-coupled receptors (GCPRs)]] could in fact induce activation of Rho, and had similar results when directly expressing activated G<sub>aq</sub>. It was already known that other [[G alpha subunit|G<sub>a</sub>]] proteins could induce Rho activation (i.e. G<sub>a</sub>13 activates p115 Rho [[Guanine nucleotide exchange factor|GEF]], which in turn activates Rho), but it was also known that G<sub>aq</sub> does not activate p115 Rho [[Guanine nucleotide exchange factor|GEF]], and therefore must act via an alternate, unknown mechanism.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Dutt |first1=P |last2=Kjoller |first2=L |last3=Giel |first3=M |last4=Hall |first4=A |last5=Toksoz |first5=D |title=Activated Galphaq family members induce Rho GTPase activation and Rho-dependent actin filament assembly. |journal=FEBS Letters |date=20 November 2002 |volume=531 |issue=3 |pages=565–569 |url=http://www.febsletters.org/article/S0014-5793(02)03625-6/abstract |doi=10.1016/s0014-5793(02)03625-6 |pmid=12435612 |bibcode=2002FEBSL.531..565D |s2cid=1712293 |url-access=subscription }}{{dead link|date=October 2016 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}</ref> Two years later, he moved to [[Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center]] as chair of the cell biology program.<ref name = "work" />

In 2005, there was an abundance of activators and targets of the Rho pathway that had been identified, yet very little investigation into the way in which specificity of the pathway is maintained. It was known at this point that several identified Rho targets were structurally similar to scaffold proteins, which have been shown in the past to mediate interaction specificity in other pathways. Hall used immunoprecipitation assays to show that CNK1, a scaffold protein-like target of Rho, interacts with two Rho-specific [[Guanine nucleotide exchange factor|GEFs]] (Net1 and p115Rho[[Guanine nucleotide exchange factor|GEF]]) and two kinases of the [[c-Jun N-terminal kinases|JNK]] [[Mitogen-activated protein kinase|MAP kinase]] pathway (MLK2 and MKK7). He then determined that CNK1 acts together with these four targets to activate the JNK MAP kinase pathway, but not other Rho-activated pathways. This led to the conclusion that CNK1 couples specific Rho exchange factors to the JNK MAP kinase pathway, providing specificity.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Jaffe|first1=AB|last2=Hall|first2=A|last3=Schmidt|first3=A|title=Association of CNK1 with Rho guanine nucleotide exchange factors controls signaling specificity downstream of Rho.|journal=Cell: Current Biology|date=8 March 2005|volume=15|issue=5|pages=405–412|doi=10.1016/j.cub.2004.12.082|pmid=15753034|s2cid=16479940|doi-access=free|bibcode=2005CBio...15..405J }}</ref> In the same year, Hall investigated the role of the small GTPase Ral in neurite branching. After microinjection of cortical and sympathetic neurons with active and dominant-negative Ral, the staining of the cells with antibodies showed that the increases in neurite branching was directly linked to the presence of active Ral. Further evidence of the importance of Ral was provided when cortical neurons were depleted of endogenous RalA and RalB isoforms by RNA interference [[RNA interference|(RNAi)]] and showed a decrease in the branching. By plating SCG on plastic dishes in the presence of different substrates, Hall realised that Ral was activated by laminin to induce this branching. In fact, Ral-dependent branching implicated the phosphorylation of growth-associated protein GAP-43. Finally, Ral mutants unable to bind to their specific effector proteins showed that RalA and RalB isoforms promote branching through exocyst complex and phospholipase D respectively.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Lalli|first1=Giovanna|last2=Hall|first2=Allan|title=Ral GTPases regulate neurite branching through GAP-43 and the exocyst complex|journal=Journal of Cell Biology|date=5 December 2005|volume=151|issue=5|pages=857–869|url=http://jcb.rupress.org/content/171/5/857.long|doi=10.1083/jcb.200507061|pmid=16330713|pmc=2171284}}</ref>

In 2010, Hall analysed a number of Rho signalling pathways, which regulate the formation of apical junctions in human bronchial epithelial (HBE) cells. Downregulation of RhoA in the HBE cell lines using [[Small interfering RNA|siRNAs]] showed a lack of apical junction formation in contrast with the controls. The siRNAs that targeted RhoA had no effect on other members of the Rho family. Further analysis showed that PRK2, a direct target of Rho, is required for the formation of apical junctions. Mutational variants of PRK2 were used to discover that although initial formation of pre-apical junctions isn't blocked, the maturation process into true apical junctions is prevented.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Wallace|first1=SW|last2=Magalhaes|first2=A|last3=Hall|first3=A|title=The Rho Target PRK2 Regulates Apical Junction Formation in Human Bronchial Epithelial Cells|journal=Molecular and Cellular Biology|date=January 2011|volume=31|issue=1|pages=81–91|doi=10.1128/MCB.01001-10|pmid=20974804|pmc=3019857}}</ref>

Hall's research has had wide implications across human health and disease, particularly cancer. In addition, a generation of cell biologists was educated and trained under his supervision across two continents.

==Honours and awards==
In 1993, Hall was awarded the Feldberg Foundation Prize for his work on the role GTP-binding proteins played on signal transduction pathways.<ref>{{Cite web|title = Prizewinners of the Feldberg Foundation|url = http://www.feldbergfoundation.org/prizewinners/|publisher = feldbergfoundation.org|accessdate = 2015-12-08}}</ref> He was elected a [[Fellow of the Academy of Medical Sciences]] in 2005.<ref name=":0" /> His work in 2005 on the regulation of adhesion, migration and polarity of the cell cytoskeleton was awarded the [[Louis-Jeantet Prize for Medicine]].<ref>{{Cite web|title = The Louis-Jeantet-Prize for Medicine 2005|url = http://www.mpg.de/510419/louis-jeantet-prize-medicine-2005|website = mpg.de|accessdate = 2015-12-08}}</ref> Later that year he won the Novartis Medal<ref>{{Cite web|title = The Novartis Medal and Prize {{!}} Biochemical Society|url = https://www.biochemistry.org/Awards/TheNovartisMedalandPrize.aspx|website = www.biochemistry.org|accessdate = 2015-12-08|archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20180901044424/https://www.biochemistry.org/Awards/TheNovartisMedalandPrize.aspx|archive-date = 1 September 2018|url-status = dead}}</ref> for his work with Rho GTPases role in cell behaviour.<ref>{{Cite journal|title = Rho GTPases and the control of cell behaviour|journal = Biochemical Society Transactions|date = 26 October 2005|issn = 0300-5127|pmid = 16246005|pages = 891–895|volume = 33|issue = 5|doi = 10.1042/BST0330891|first = A.|last = Hall}}</ref> The [[Canada Gairdner International Award]] (2006) was awarded to him for the discovery of Rho GTPases that play a role in cytoskeleton arrangement and cell migration and its application to cancerous cells.<ref>{{Cite web|title = Alan Hall {{!}} Gairdner|url = http://www.gairdner.org/content/alan-hall|website = www.gairdner.org|accessdate = 2015-12-08}}</ref>
